desc:
A flat-topped mountain consists of three consecutive parts: a non-empty strictly increasing run, then a plateau of one or more equal values (the top), then a non-empty strictly decreasing run. The plateau value is larger than the value before it and larger than the value after it.

Given such an array nums, return the width of the plateau, that is, how many elements are equal to the maximum.

For example, in [1, 3, 7, 7, 7, 4, 2] the plateau is 7, 7, 7, so the answer is 3. Aim for O(log n) time even when the plateau is huge.
constraints: nums consists of a strictly increasing run, a plateau of at least one element, and a strictly decreasing run; the two runs are not empty
hints: Counting the elements equal to the maximum is O(n). Since the plateau is a contiguous block, you only need to find where it starts and where it ends.
The plateau starts at the first index i where nums[i] < nums[i + 1] is no longer true. The plateau ends before the first index whose value is smaller than the plateau value.

Run two binary searches. First find the start s (the climb test nums[mid] < nums[mid + 1] is true before it, false from it). Then search the range [s, n - 1] for the first index e with nums[e] < nums[s]; the width is e - s.
editorial: Both ends of the plateau are boundaries of a predicate that changes value exactly once, so each is found by a binary search.

Start of the plateau: the predicate 'nums[i] < nums[i + 1]' (still climbing) is true on the increasing run and false at the first plateau element (and everywhere after). Binary search on [0, n - 1] with lo = mid + 1 when it is true and hi = mid otherwise gives the first index where it is false, which is the plateau start s. Because the increasing run is strictly increasing and non-empty, and the plateau is followed by a strictly lower value, no other position can fool this test.

End of the plateau: from index s on, the predicate 'nums[i] < nums[s]' is false on the plateau and true after it, since the final run is strictly decreasing. A second binary search on [s, n] finds the first index e where it holds (or n if none), and the plateau has e - s elements.
Total time is O(log n) and extra space O(1), independent of the plateau width. A linear count would degrade to O(n).
